title: Sound and Efficient Certification of High-Quality Qubit Operations: Theory and Experiment
authors: Nikolai Miklin, Jan Nöller, José Martínez, Lucas B. Vieira, Ulrich Poschinger, Ferdinand Schmidt-Kaler, Mariami Gachechiladze
abstract: Can a high-quality quantum gate be certified when uncharacterized state-preparation and measurement errors are dominant? Can this be achieved with low experimental overhead? Here, we introduce a sound black-box certification protocol for a single-qubit gate based on a small set of fixed, deterministic sequences. From the data, the protocol derives finite-sample bounds on the gate's rotation eigenvalue, a gauge-invariant property. Its phase reveals the accuracy of the rotation angle, while its modulus quantifies the loss of coherence under repeated gate applications. We implement the protocol on a $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^{+}$ trapped-ion processor and certify the $\sqrt{\mathrm{X}}$-gate rotation eigenvalue using $22\,000$ circuit executions, and demonstrate the robustness of certification to state-preparation and measurement errors by deliberately degrading the readout. Finally, we prove that these spectral constraints imply, up to a physically meaningful unitary change of basis, a rigorous average gate-fidelity lower bound for every time-independent qubit model compatible with the data. In both readout settings, the spectral bounds yield the same fidelity certificate of $99.94(3)\%$ with $99\%$ confidence. Our results establish a new standard for quantum-gate certification by combining soundness and experimental efficiency without requiring trusted reference operations, randomized circuits, or model fitting.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, sound, and efficient black-box protocol to certify the quality of single-qubit quantum gates, even when state-preparation and measurement errors are unknown. By analyzing deterministic sequences, the authors derive bounds on the gate's rotation eigenvalue, which quantifies both angular and coherence errors. The method was successfully demonstrated on a trapped-ion quantum processor, setting a new standard for hardware characterization.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of certifying the quality of single-qubit quantum gates when the underlying state-preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors are unknown and dominant.
main_result: They established a sound, efficient black-box certification protocol that successfully certified a high-fidelity $\sqrt{X}$-gate on a trapped-ion processor, achieving a fidelity certificate of $99.94(3)\%$ with $99\%$ confidence.
method: The protocol uses a small set of fixed, deterministic sequences to derive finite-sample bounds on the gate's rotation eigenvalue ($\lambda$), which is a gauge-invariant property.
model_or_system: The experiment was implemented on a $^{40}	ext{Ca}^{+}$ trapped-ion processor, modeling the gate operation via an unknown quantum channel $\Lambda$ acting on the qubit state.
key_observables: Rotation eigenvalue ($\lambda$), which has a phase (angle error) and a modulus (coherence loss); error probability $\epsilon_n$.
important_parameters: Fidelity lower bound ($F_{	ext{avg}}$); confidence level ($99\%$); number of circuit executions ($22,000$).
main_assumptions: The derived spectral constraints imply a rigorous average gate-fidelity lower bound for any time-independent qubit model compatible with the data, without requiring trusted reference operations or model fitting.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the protocol using Bloch sphere representations and the target circuit; Figure 2 shows experimental estimates of the error probability $\epsilon_n$ versus sequence length $n$ for different noise regimes.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the theoretical framework for black-box certification, details the two-stage measurement protocol (preliminary test followed by refined analysis of $\epsilon_n$), presents the theoretical bounds on $\lambda$, and concludes with experimental validation on the trapped-ion platform.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly practical and theoretically rigorous method for benchmarking quantum hardware, which is crucial for advancing fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.
